\chapter{Hay Que --- Somebody Has To, and Nobody in Particular}
\label{ch:hay-que}
\hlchaptermodality{170}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can express an obligation without naming who is obliged.}

Complete ES-C54-hay-que: produce hay que hablar espanol and name the other construction that leaves the person out.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[hay que]{hay que — somebody has to, and nobody in particular}

\label{lesson:ES-C54-hay-que}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Se habla español} left the person out. So did every sign you read. Here is the other way Spanish does that — and this one is about obligation.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: an obligation with nobody in it}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{hay que} + a plain infinitive — \emph{one must}, \emph{you have to}, \emph{it is necessary to}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{\textbf{Hay que} hablar español.} — You have to speak Spanish. \emph{\textbf{Hay que} comer.} — One must eat.
\end{quote}

Three words you already own, and no new grammar: \emph{hay}, \emph{que}, and a verb in its dictionary form.

What it produces is an obligation with \textbf{nobody obliged}. \emph{Hay que hablar español} does not say who has to — not you, not me, not them. It says the requirement exists, the way a sign says a thing is forbidden without saying who forbids it.

That is the same move as the impersonal \emph{se}, and now you have both:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{Spanish} & \textbf{leaves out} \\
\midrule
something happens & \emph{se habla español} & who does it \\
something must happen & \emph{hay que hablar español} & who must \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Two constructions, one habit: \textbf{Spanish is comfortable saying that something is the case without saying who is behind it.} English needs a vague \emph{you} or \emph{they} or a passive to manage the same thing, and always sounds slightly like it is avoiding the question.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}Hay que hablar español\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}Se habla español\textquotedblright{} — both with nobody in them
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\textquotedblleft{}One must eat\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{Hay que comer}}.) Who must? (\textbf{Nobody named.}) And which other construction does the same? (The \textbf{impersonal \emph{se}}.) Next: all of it in one place.
\end{tcolorbox}
